articles.title: Buracos e descarte irregular de lixo transformam estrada rural em PP | G1
articles.standfirst: Moradores e proprietários de sítios denunciam as condições da estrada Bom Pastor, devido ao entulho acumulado em córrego. A situação também preocupa devido aos possíveis danos ambientais.
articles.summary: Os moradores e proprietários de sítios denunciam as condições da estrada Bom Pastor, em Presidente Prudente (SP), devido aos buracos e descarte irregular de lixo.
articles.body:
Moradores e proprietários de sítios denunciam que a estrada rural Bom Pastor, em Presidente Prudente (SP), virou um problema por conta dos buracos e do descarte irregular de lixo.

O problema relatado pelos moradores está voltado à má conservação da via e possíveis danos ambientais em uma área de preservação.

Segundo relatos enviados à TV TEM , uma antiga ponte de madeira sobre um córrego se deteriorou por falta de manutenção e precisou ser substituída após uma intervenção da Defesa Civil. No entanto, em vez da construção de uma nova estrutura adequada, a prefeitura teria instalado dutos de concreto e utilizado restos de materiais de construção e entulhos para formar a passagem.

Os moradores afirmam que o local passou a acumular lixo, pedaços de colchão, vaso sanitário e outros resíduos da construção civil. Com as chuvas, parte desses materiais estaria sendo arrastada pela enxurrada em direção ao leito do córrego, aumentando a preocupação com a contaminação ambiental.

Buracos e descarte irregular de lixo transformam estrada rural em problema em Prudente (SP) — Foto: Aceituno Jr./TV TEM

A área, que antes apresentava vegetação e características naturais, teria sido bastante descaracterizada. “Nós não podemos jogar nada na beira do rio porque diz que dá poluição, mas olha quantos sacos de lixo. Tudo o que já colocaram, a água levou para o riozinho e tudo é poluição”, lamentou o produtor rural Darci Delmar.

“Aqui, se não tiver uma estrada boa, fica difícil. Tem muita gente que depende e precisa ir e voltar quase todos os dias para a cidade”, continuou o morador.

A instrutora de equitação, Roberta Junqueira, reforçou que os cascalhos utilizados na ponte estão assoreando o rio. “Quando acontece a chuva, o gado fica ilhado para um canto, não tem como a gente manusear o gado para o outro lado.”

“Além da passagem, as propriedades em volta estão sofrendo com isso. Inclusive, os entulhos assorearam e abarrancaram tudo em volta. Então tem árvore caindo em volta, os bambus estão caindo em volta, estão aumentando o leito do rio e desbarrancando, e os próprios entulhos que estão fazendo isso”, reforçou a moradora.

Buracos e descarte irregular de lixo transformam estrada rural em problema em Prudente — Foto: Aceituno Jr./TV TEM

Além disso, a Estrada Bom Pastor apresenta diversos buracos ao longo do trajeto, dificultando o trânsito e colocando em risco quem utiliza a via diariamente.

Os moradores ressaltam que o trecho não atende apenas proprietários de sítios de lazer, mas também famílias e trabalhadores que dependem da estrada para se deslocar.

Atualmente, a passagem construída no lugar da antiga ponte ainda permite a circulação de veículos, segundo uma moradora, mas a situação é considerada precária.

Os moradores cobram providências da prefeitura para recuperar a estrada, garantir uma travessia segura e retirar os resíduos descartados na área, com destinação ambientalmente adequada.

A prefeitura disse à TV TEM que iria enviar equipes para retirar os entulhos de maior volume, mas não definiu uma data exata. Sobre o estado de conservação da estrada, a prefeitura informou que melhorias estão previstas, mas não informou quando isso deverá acontecer.

articles.title: Bolsonaro está clinicamente estável e segue em UTI, diz boletim médico | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-presidente está internado em unidade de terapia intensiva com o diagnóstico de abdômen agudo obstrutivo.
articles.summary: Ex-presidente está internado em unidade de terapia intensiva com o diagnóstico de abdômen agudo obstrutivo.
articles.body:
Ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro — Foto: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

O ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro está clinicamente estável, informou o Hospital DF Star na tarde deste domingo (22). Bolsonaro está internado na unidade de terapia intensiva (UTI) com diagnóstico de abdômen agudo obstrutivo. Segundo o boletim médico, não há previsão de alta.

O informe diz, ainda, que Jair Bolsonaro mantém "tratamento clínico, jejum e suporte nutricional".

O boletim médico é assinado pelos médicos Brasil Caiado (cardiologista), Leandro Echenique (cardiologista), Claudio Birolini (cirurgião do aparelho digestivo), Antonio Aurélio Fagundes Junior (coordenador da UTI Geral) e Allisson Barcelos Borges (diretor-geral do hospital).

🔎 Atualmente, Bolsonaro cumpre uma pena de 27 anos e 3 meses de prisão após ser condenado por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Desde 24 de março deste ano ele está em prisão domiciliar humanitária, autorizada pelo ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF).

Desde que começou a cumprir a pena, em novembro de 2025, Bolsonaro esteve internado no hospital DF Star diversas vezes.

Neste sábado, Moraes atendeu a um pedido da defesa e autorizou que três filhos de Jair Bolsonaro — Carlos, Jair Renan e a filha menor de idade — possam visitá-lo diariamente enquanto durar sua internação.

Na decisão, Moraes ressaltou que as visitas precisam seguir as regras internas do hospital e que está proibida a entrada de "celulares, câmeras ou quaisquer outros aparelhos eletrônicos que possam registrar imagens ou áudios.

Brasília, 22 de novembro de 2026 – O hospital DF Star informa que o expresidente da república Jair Messias Bolsonaro encontra-se internado em unidade de terapia intensiva com o diagnóstico de abdômen agudo obstrutivo. Paciente apresenta-se clinicamente estável, mantendo tratamento clínico, jejum e suporte nutricional. Segue sem previsão de alta hospitalar.

articles.title: $275M Obama-era solar fraud case could net taxpayers $1B, but Trump's DOJ backs Biden dismissal
articles.summary: Investors behind a False Claims Act qui tam lawsuit over Crescent Dunes' $275 million federal grant say the Trump DOJ is defending a Biden-era dismissal.
articles.body: This article is Part 2 of a Fox News Digital exclusive series investigating the Crescent Dunes solar power plant in Nevada. You can read Part 1 here. The Trump administration has made fighting fraud and rooting out government waste a top priority, even offering cash rewards to Americans who expose wrongdoing. Yet investors in a failed Obama-era solar plant are questioning why President Donald Trump's own Justice Department is fighting to squash their fraud lawsuit over a $275 million federal grant — a case they say could recover up to $1 billion for taxpayers. The investors allege that Spanish construction giant ACS and companies to tied its former subsidiary Cobra, misled federal officials into approving the grant by claiming the troubled solar plant was ready for use, even though it had suffered major construction problems and was shut down for months following a molten-salt-tank failure. The lawsuit centers on the beleaguered Crescent Dunes solar plant, a billion-dollar, government-backed project that began operating in Nevada in 2015 but was later plagued by engineering failures, repeated shutdowns and two bankruptcies before being sold for just $7 million in July. HOW A $1B OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT WENT BANKRUPT TWICE, LEAVING TAXPAYERS WITH THE TAB The plant was built around an emerging solar technology that used thousands of mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a towering receiver, heating molten salt that could be stored and used to generate electricity even after sunset. In 2020, a group of private investors who had put $90 million into the project and suffered substantial losses filed a whistleblower lawsuit, alleging the companies had misled the federal government to secure the enormous grant. But in November 2024, just two days after Trump's re-election, Biden's Justice Department moved to shut down the lawsuit, arguing that pursuing the case would burden federal agencies. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES The incoming Trump administration could have reconsidered that position in early 2025. Instead, its Justice Department defended the Biden-era dismissal in an April filing with a federal appeals court. CMB, an investment group headed by Pat Hogan, is appealing the dismissal. Hogan is also urging Trump’s Justice Department to ask the court to reopen the case. "It makes no sense," Hogan told Fox News Digital in a video interview. Hogan said he had contacted Trump's Justice Department seeking help reviving the case but had received no commitment. "The real problem here is, why isn't the government asking for this?" he said. "All in all, I would say this has just been a fleecing of the federal government by a foreign entity. And we have the opportunity to fix it, and they're doing nothing." Hogan argues that allowing the lawsuit to proceed could potentially net hundreds of millions of dollars for taxpayers. Under the False Claims Act, which CMB used to bring its lawsuit, companies found liable can face damages of up to three times the government's proven losses, plus additional penalties. "This could be a billion dollars," Hogan said. Tonopah Solar Energy, the plant's former owner and one of the defendants, has rejected CMB's allegations as baseless in court filings. Other companies named in the lawsuit have also backed the Justice Department's effort to dismiss the case. In an April 2026 court filing, Trump's Justice Department defended the Biden administration's decision, making the same argument that continuing the lawsuit would drain government resources and that federal law gave it broad authority to shut down the case. In court filings reviewed by Fox News Digital, neither administration put a dollar figure on the cost of continuing the lawsuit. The decision has left Hogan and his investors questioning why the government shut down the case — and what Treasury officials knew about the plant's serious problems when they approved the $275 million grant. What CMB alleges happened At the heart of the lawsuit is a dispute over whether Crescent Dunes was properly completed — and whether its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, was entitled to collect the $275 million Treasury grant. The grant was part of a $26 billion program within the Obama administration's broader $90 billion green-energy push, launched under the 2009 economic stimulus package to create jobs and turbocharge its green energy agenda. Known as Section 1603, the program paid developers about 30% of their qualifying construction costs once their facilities were "placed in service" — meaning ready and available for their intended use. Treasury considered several factors in determining whether a plant met that standard, including whether it had passed critical tests, begun generating electricity and come under its owner's control. Crescent Dunes began generating electricity in 2015, but CMB alleges it had produced no more than 32% of its expected output through June 2016. Then, in October 2016, a failure involving the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank shut it down for months. In December, while Crescent Dunes was still shut down, its builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, formally handed the plant over to its owner, Tonopah Solar Energy, under an arrangement known as "provisional acceptance." But first, they changed the construction contract to allow the handover despite major defects and unfinished repairs. That agreement came just days before the year-end deadline for solar plants to be ready for use to qualify for the Treasury grants. In a later court filing, CMB alleged that more than 9,000 defects had been identified and grouped into roughly 500 outstanding construction items, including seven major deficiencies. The investors argue the problems showed the plant was not ready to be handed over. The December agreement itself acknowledged that repairs to the failed hot molten-salt storage tank were still needed. The tank was central to the plant's operation, storing heat from the sun so electricity could be generated even after sunset. CMB alleges the companies used the revised agreement to make Crescent Dunes appear ready for use and secure the Treasury grant, even though major problems remained unresolved. What Washington knew - and when Records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Treasury had questioned whether Crescent Dunes was ready for use months before approving the grant payment. In September 2016, Treasury questioned a claim by Tonopah Solar Energy that Crescent Dunes had been ready for use since February of that year. The agency pointed to a July commissioning report suggesting the builder, Cobra Thermosolar Plants, had not yet formally handed control of the facility over to Tonopah. In a Sept. 21 response to Treasury's questions, Tonopah Solar Energy defended its claim, arguing that the plant had passed key tests and was capable of generating electricity. It also acknowledged an earlier extended shutdown caused by problems with the plant's salt-piping system. The following month, the plant's hot molten-salt storage tank failed, forcing the plant offline for months. Despite that breakdown, Tonopah and Cobra went ahead with the revised handover agreement in December. On March 7, 2017, just weeks into the first Trump administration, Treasury approved a $243.7 million grant payment — even though Crescent Dunes remained shut down nearly five months after the tank failure. The plant would not resume generating electricity until July 2017. The approval letter said Treasury was still reviewing some of the project's claimed costs before deciding whether to release additional money. In February 2018, Treasury approved an additional $31.9 million, bringing the total grant awards to approximately $275.6 million, according to newly obtained federal records. The additional payment was scheduled for disbursement within seven business days. But Treasury was not the only federal agency involved. The Department of Energy, which had backed Crescent Dunes with a $737 million federal loan guarantee, also had a say in major construction decisions. DOE approved the revised December handover despite unfinished repairs. It also waived certain missed deadlines, allowing the plant to be formally recognized as operational under its loan agreement. That approval did not automatically qualify Crescent Dunes for the separate Treasury grant. A separate December 2016 financing agreement involving Tonopah Solar Energy and DOE required the Treasury grant money to go first toward repaying the project’s short-term federal borrowing, including principal and accrued interest. Documents obtained by Fox News Digital show that Tonopah Solar Energy made a $218.9 million payment toward a federal loan in March 2017, shortly after Treasury approved its initial grant award. "So in a sense, the federal government just paid themselves, right? So they're still out the money, right," Hogan told Fox News Digital. On April 12, 2017, while Crescent Dunes was still offline, DOE published an article celebrating the plant as a breakthrough in solar technology without mentioning that it had been shut down for months. What remains unclear is whether Treasury officials knew about the October breakdown, unfinished repairs and December contract changes when they authorized the initial grant payment — information that could have affected whether the plant qualified for the grant. Fox News Digital has asked DOE and Treasury about the grant's approval process, the plant's condition and taxpayer losses, but neither agency has provided a full accounting. In a statement, the Trump administration's Department of Energy criticized previous administrations' handling of the project, saying it had resolved its financial interests in Crescent Dunes in 2020. "It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green New Scam," a DOE spokesperson said. "Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project." Fox News Digital has also filed Freedom of Information Act requests seeking grant payment records, loan accounting and communications between the agencies. Why the DOJ shut down the lawsuit In January 2020, Hogan's investment group, CMB, which had lent $90 million to a company tied to Crescent Dunes developer SolarReserve, sued Tonopah Solar Energy and companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, accusing them of defrauding the federal government. The lawsuit was filed under the False Claims Act, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on the government's behalf and receive a share of any money recovered. Known as "qui tam" cases, the lawsuits can be taken over or dismissed by the Justice Department. After investigating CMB's allegations for more than three years, Biden's Justice Department declined to take over the lawsuit in June 2023, leaving CMB to pursue it alone. On Nov. 7, 2024, just two days after Trump's election victory, Biden's Justice Department moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that continuing the case would burden the Treasury, Energy and Justice departments. CMB challenged the move, arguing that Biden's DOJ had failed to explain what had changed since it allowed the investors to proceed. Then, in July 2025, six months into Trump's second term, a federal judge granted DOJ's request and dismissed the lawsuit without deciding whether the fraud allegations were true. CMB appealed to the Ninth Circuit, where Trump's Justice Department defended the dismissal in an April 2026 court filing. Matt Dunn, an attorney at Covington & Burling who specializes in False Claims Act litigation, described DOJ's decision to intervene after initially allowing the case to proceed as "unusual, but not extraordinary." Dunn said the government may have its own assessment of a lawsuit's potential value that differs from the whistleblower's. "The government might privately have a different view of the merits of the case or the potential value of the case that it doesn't necessarily share publicly," Dunn said. WATCH: Physicist explains why bankrupt Obama-era solar plant failed, calls it a ‘boondoggle’ Dunn said the Supreme Court has given the government substantial discretion to dismiss such cases, describing the legal hurdle for whistleblowers seeking to overturn a dismissal as "an extraordinarily high bar for a relator to overcome." Hogan, meanwhile, has a financial stake in the outcome. He says his investors lost the $90 million they lent to the SolarReserve-linked company. If the lawsuit is revived and CMB ultimately succeeds, the government theoretically could recover up to three times its proven damages under the False Claims Act, and CMB could receive a share, potentially offsetting its investors' losses. "That's my job for my investors to leave no stone unturned to try to make sure that, in fact, I get their money back," Hogan said. The Ninth Circuit must now decide whether the lawsuit can move forward — potentially opening the door for the government to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in disputed funds — or whether DOJ's decision to shut it down will stand. Congress demands answers The Justice Department's handling of the case has also drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill. In February 2025, Reps. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, and Carol Miller, R-W.Va., urged Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate why the Biden administration moved to shut down the lawsuit. Gooden later urged Secretary of War Pete Hegseth to consider suspending federal contracts with companies tied to Spanish construction giant ACS, whose subsidiary Cobra built the plant and held a stake in Tonopah Solar Energy. He also called for an investigation into ACS and Banco Santander's roles in the project's financing and bankruptcy amid the allegations of fraud involving federal funds. "When taxpayers are defrauded to a scale this massive, our government has a responsibility to get the facts and hold those responsible to account," Gooden told Fox News Digital. "That is why I have asked Secretary Hegseth to pause contracts with ACS-affiliated entities until these allegations are fully reviewed and every avenue to recover taxpayer money has been pursued." One such contract involves a $2.84 billion Navy dry dock project at Pearl Harbor awarded to a joint venture involving ACS subsidiary Dragados. The project completion date has been delayed from September 2027 to March 2029, according to the Government Accountability Office. Dragados is not accused of fraud in the Crescent Dunes lawsuit. Miller, meanwhile, also questioned how a project backed by nearly $1 billion in federal financing could end up selling for $7 million. "That's not good math," Miller told Fox News Digital. She suggested another congressional letter could be warranted, saying that "if we can recover any of that taxpayer money, that would be wonderful." In April 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, a longtime defender of whistleblowers who helped strengthen the False Claims Act in 1986, demanded answers from DOJ over its handling of fraud lawsuits, particularly cases it shut down despite whistleblowers wanting to press ahead. In a July 10 response obtained by Fox News Digital, DOJ revealed that Crescent Dunes was one of just 12 cases in which it moved to shut down a lawsuit after initially allowing it to proceed — fewer than 0.3% of nearly 5,000 whistleblower cases received between 2020 and 2025. DOJ also confirmed that other federal agencies can push to have such lawsuits dismissed, including to avoid the burden of producing evidence. But it did not say whether Treasury or DOE pushed to kill the Crescent Dunes case — or what investigators found when they examined the fraud allegations. The defense and unanswered questions The companies accused of fraud have backed DOJ's effort to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that federal law gives the government broad authority to shut down whistleblower cases. Tonopah Solar Energy, which filed for bankruptcy in January 2026, has also fiercely rejected CMB's allegations, accusing the investors of pursuing a "scorched earth mission" through repeated legal challenges against the company. "The reality is there is no merit to CMB's claims whatsoever," the company argued in an April 2026 bankruptcy filing. Tonopah Solar Energy made those arguments while winding down its affairs in bankruptcy, before selling the plant's assets in July. The new owners had no involvement in the alleged 2016 fraud, and the bankruptcy sale generally shielded them from the former owner's legal liabilities. In a separate 2020 lawsuit, Hogan's investors sought to recover an allegedly unpaid $90 million loan, suing companies tied to Crescent Dunes after SolarReserve failed to repay much of the money. They suffered a setback in 2024 when an arbitration panel rejected five of their claims and ordered them to pay $2.44 million in legal fees and costs. The companies did not respond to Fox News Digital's repeated requests for comment. The dispute was separate from the whistleblower lawsuit alleging fraud involving the $275 million Treasury grant. Despite years of investigation, the Justice Department has never publicly disclosed what it uncovered. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Nearly seven years after Hogan's investors filed their lawsuit, the fraud allegations have never been tested at trial. And despite President Trump's pledge to crack down on fraud and wasteful green-energy spending, his Justice Department is still defending the Biden administration's decision to shut down the case. "If we're wrong, the evidence will show it," Hogan said. "But don't let a Biden-era dismissal prevent the merits from ever being heard."

articles.title: Newsom's bid to empty California's death row collides with voters' repeated rejection of abolition
articles.summary: A lawsuit challenges Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's effort to commute all 548 death sentences, citing failures to notify district attorneys.
articles.body: A lawsuit challenging Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to commute 548 death sentences is raising questions about the governor's clemency powers, with a legal expert arguing Newsom is using his gubernatorial authority to circumvent the will of voters who have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish capital punishment. Newsom announced Nov. 5 that he intends to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the Golden State's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that will take effect only after the necessary legal steps are completed. The Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF) on Sunday filed a lawsuit at the California Supreme Court seeking to block Newsom's proposed sweeping commutation, citing the governor's "failure to provide legally required notice to district attorneys and his disregard for the rights of victims and their families to be notified and heard," according to a news release. Newsom may be using clemency to impose his own views on capital punishment despite voters repeatedly rejecting abolition, Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for Courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital on Tuesday. MICHAEL RUIZ: DA IDENTIFIES 49 LOCAL KILLERS SLATED FOR NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW CLEMENCY — AND THEIR CRIMES "The death penalty remains on the books in California, and as you alluded to, California voters have repeatedly rejected efforts to abolish the death penalty," Smith said. "So Californians understand that it can be an appropriate punishment in certain circumstances. Now, [Gov.] Newsom, he does have the ability to exercise the pardon, the commutation power, the contours of that obviously are being litigated, but I think what's clear is that from a practical standpoint, [Gov.] Newsom is essentially using this to circumvent the clear will of the voters and impose his own views of the death penalty over those of ... the California populace." "Now some of the specifics related to this suit challenging Gavin Newsom's use of the commutation pardon, that is going to vary a little bit from state to state," Smith added. "So this is going focus largely on issues of California state law and the issues specifically that I think will get the most attention is whether the California Supreme Court would essentially have to weigh in and more or less approve some of these repeat offenders before their sentences can be commuted." California voters notably defeated Proposition 34, a ballot initiative to ban capital punishment, in 2012, according to Ballotpedia. Voters in the Golden State similarly rejected Proposition 62, the Abolition of Death Penalty Measure, in November 2016, per Ballotpedia. The lawsuit alleges that Newsom "has claimed to himself the unfettered power to decide how clemency should be granted, ignored the Legislature’s requirement of a referral to the Board of Parole Hearings for investigation and recommendation, ignored the role of the trial court and District Attorney in providing crucial factual input to the Board of Parole Hearings, ignored the limitation of the required notice to District Attorneys, and deprived the Legislature, the public, and this Court of the information needed to determine whether he has abused his authority." CJLF's lawsuit also requests that "the Court immediately stay any issuance, implementation, recognition, or enforcement of the challenged commutations pending further order of the Court and pending determination of this petition on the merits." Anne Marie Schubert, president and CEO of CJLF, said in a statement that the lawsuit "is about protecting the constitutional rights of victims, defending the rule of law, and ensuring that no Governor is above the law." "The Governor’s clemency power does not authorize mass commutations that disregard constitutional safeguards, legally required procedures, or victims’ rights," Schubert said, adding that "blanket commutation is not an exercise of discretion — it is an abandonment of it." CJLF and Newsom's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The coalition suing Newsom is comprised of several law enforcement leaders and organizations, victims’ rights groups and multiple district attorneys, including Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho, who ran as a Democrat in the 2026 congressional primary. Some of California’s most notorious serial killers are among the death row inmates whose sentences Newsom plans to commute, KTLA reported Nov. 8. "Obviously, these are individuals who, again, have been convicted by a jury of their peers of committing particularly aggravated forms of murder," Smith told Fox News Digital. "Again, many of these individuals tortured their victims and included sexual violence against their victims before they were ultimately killed. And so these are individuals that their own peers thought deserved the death penalty. And, so again, to see [Gov.] Newsom circumventing this through his commutation power is very, very troubling." Under the California Constitution, Newsom must obtain a recommendation from at least four California Supreme Court justices before commuting the sentences of 382 inmates who have been convicted of more than one felony. The California Supreme Court has invited interested parties to weigh in on the proposed commutations, with legal briefs due Nov. 24 and Newsom's response due Dec. 4. Attorney General Rob Bonta told the court Newsom will not formally commute any death sentences until the justices act, including those of inmates with only one felony conviction. Newsom's office has argued that the governor's broad constitutional clemency authority allows him to initiate blanket commutations without following statutory procedures governing individual applications, while separately seeking the California Supreme Court's required recommendation for inmates with multiple felony convictions. CALIFORNIA DA SAYS GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'CRUEL' DEATH ROW CLEMENCY STABS CRIME VICTIMS 'IN THE HEART' "District attorneys have a legal responsibility to represent the people of California and protect the rights of crime victims," Greg Totten, CEO of the California District Attorneys Association, said in a statement. "The Governor’s failure to provide legally required notice to prosecutors has deprived them of the opportunity to provide critical information and ensure that victims and their families are heard." 'BABY KILLERS, COP KILLERS' HAVE AN ALLY IN NEWSOM, MURDERED GIRL'S FATHER SAYS AMID DEATH ROW CONTROVERSY "No Governor should be permitted to circumvent the very safeguards designed to ensure that justice is served," Totten added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Newsom's proposed commutations would mark the largest mass commutation of death sentences in American history, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Newsom also issued a March 2019 executive order establishing a moratorium on executions in California, leaving the state's death penalty law and existing death sentences in place. Democratic California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said in a May 28, 2026, X post that he plans to extend California’s moratorium on executions when he takes office. "Governor Newsom’s death penalty moratorium represented an important step toward a more just criminal justice system," Becerra wrote in the post. "As Governor, I will extend California’s moratorium on executions and continue moving our state away from a costly, flawed system that disproportionately impacts Black and brown communities and too often gets it wrong." Dan Dow, district attorney of San Luis Obispo County, California, blasted Newsom's proposed commutation as "a sickening abuse of power" in a Nov. 5 statement. "Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California's 548 condemned killers that the killers' lives matter more," Dow asserted. "Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power."

articles.title: 'Crazy': Moderates fear Dem leadership promised far-left reparations and ICE demands in turn of votes
articles.summary: House Democrats are split as progressives' push to abolish ICE and reparations for descendants of slavery, while moderates warn it may hurt affordability.
articles.body: Progressive House Democrats believe party leaders could use their newly won majority to back their far-left agenda on such matters as reparations and abolishing ICE, despite pushback from moderates concerned about the party's direction. Newly elected Democratic Caucus Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and progressive lawmakers told Fox News Digital that proposals to abolish ICE, expand deportation protections and pursue slavery reparations will be part of the party's legislative discussions under Speaker-nominee Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., despite concerns from moderates that the agenda could distract from affordability. ‘SQUAD’ MEMBER ANNOUNCES ‘MAJORITY PRIORITIES’ INCLUDING REPARATIONS, ABOLISHING ICE AFTER BLUE WAVE "Jeffries has been very clear, he wants to make sure everyone in the caucus is well represented," Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, told Fox News Digital. Lieu told Fox News Digital that he is "excited" to have "discussions on everything" with members of the caucus, including proposals involving reparations and abolishing ICE. The California Democrat said he would also be willing to consider other priorities of Rep. Ayanna Presley, D-Mass., including Medicare for All, "abortion justice" and extending Temporary Protected Status for Third World migrants. 'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., a prominent supporter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), told Fox News Digital that progressives and Jeffries have found common ground on several priorities outlined in Pressley's agenda, including expanding healthcare access and public housing. "Of course, there are going to be areas where leader Jeffries and DSA are going to be in strong opposition, but there are also areas like expanding Medicaid, public housing, and housing issues in general, where there are shared values that unite everybody," Ocasio-Cortez, a potential 2028 presidential contender, told Fox News Digital. Ocasio-Cortez has also begun working with Democratic leadership on the House Energy and Commerce Committee to advance her healthcare priorities, a senior congressional democratic staffer told Fox News Digital. However, moderate Democrats were skeptical that party leadership would embrace the progressive agenda, with some questioning whether Jeffries and other leaders had promised to consider those demands in exchange for support during the leadership elections. "Our agenda is to focus on costs," Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital. "What's clear is we had an overwhelming majority. I think some of my colleagues seem to be unhappy with winning in a place we've never won before." Gottheimer accused progressive colleagues of wanting to "squawk and complain and make their demands" rather than focus on the issues that helped Democrats win the midterm elections. The New Jersey Democrat also rejected proposals to "defund police, have open borders, or get rid of the United States Senate," arguing that neither he nor Democratic leadership would support such policies. HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' Gottheimer, an outspoken critic of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), suggested that Pressley's priorities more closely resemble the organization's platform than the broader Democratic Party's agenda. "The DSA, they have their own agenda," Gottheimer said. RADICAL SOCIALIST WING'S HUGE NIGHT REVEALS ASCENDING CLOUT WITHIN DEMOCRATIC PARTY Another Democratic lawmaker, who requested anonymity, told Fox News Digital that they and a longtime colleague viewed the prospect of leadership adopting the progressive agenda as "crazy." The lawmaker also speculated that Lieu and Jeffries were expressing openness to progressive proposals to avoid opposition during Wednesday's leadership elections. articles.title: Trump says it will be 'very hard' to work with Schumer after he predicted deals
articles.summary: Trump said it would be "very hard" to work with Schumer if he leads the Senate next year, days after the president said he could make deals with Democrats.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump criticized Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-New York, two days after he said he could strike key deals with Democrats who will hold majorities in both the House and Senate next year.

"It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader. He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again," Trump said Nov. 22 in a Truth Social post .

Still, Trump last week called both Schumer and likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries "smart" and added that he could negotiate compromises with them on health care, immigration and other top issues. "If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too," Trump said at the White House Nov. 20.

Schumer served as Senate majority leader during former President Joe Biden 's term in the White House, but he now faces a challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has received support from parts of the moderate and progressive wings of the party.

Trump says deals possible with Democrats on health care, immigration

Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a centrist, and her future colleague, progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, have pledged to support Van Hollen, as have other Senate members of the party's left flank.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, and incoming Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan have all pledged to support Van Hollen.

Trump also chided Schumer in his Truth Social post about the 2016 presidential election, appearing to reference the Senate Intel Committee's investigation into Russian interference . The president accused the now-Senate minority leader of perpetrating "hoaxes and scams."

USA TODAY reached out to Schumer's office for comment.

During his Nov. 20 news conference, Trump said he would likely begin the next Congress with a veto pen in hand, but he also previewed potential dealmaking.

"They're going to send things my way and I'm going to veto them," Trump said. "But I think after a month or so they're going to send things and I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this."

articles.title: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed says he’s open to working with the Trump administration
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said he’s open to working with Trump on an agenda to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans, just weeks after the three men lobbed attacks on each other during a tense campaign season.
articles.body: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said Sunday that he’s open to working with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans, just weeks after the three men lobbed verbal attacks at each other during a tense campaign. Asked whether he intended to meet with the president or vice president soon, El-Sayed told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that “plans are in the works.” “As I said, I’m open to speaking with anybody. I’m the senator-elect for the state of Michigan. My people, the people in the state, elected me to serve them, and I’ll work with anyone who’s ready to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All,” El-Sayed added, repeating a refrain from his campaign. “I’m looking forward to those conversations about what we can do together, whether it’s with Democrats or Republicans.” Multiple times while campaigning for El-Sayed’s opponent, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, Trump labeled the then-Democratic Senate nominee a “jihadist” and referred to him by his middle name, “Mohamed.” El-Sayed accused the president and his allies of Islamophobia in the wake of these attacks. In his victory speech on election night, the senator-elect addressed the president directly, saying, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.” One of the key proposals from the senator-elect’s campaign for Senate was to pass a measure that would guarantee healthcare for Americans “from cradle to grave.” On Saturday, he engaged with Trump on social media with a post on X suggesting that new healthcare legislation could be named, “Trumpcare.” “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave,” El-Sayed wrote, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “Trumpcare” inscribed on it. The president later posted the image on his own social media account, but didn’t add his own comments. On Sunday, the vice president’s team confirmed that they were informed that El-Sayed is interested in meeting with Vance and that Vance’s office reached out to El-Sayed’s team to set up a meeting. In an interview on Fox News on Saturday, Trump said he would be open to working with Democrats on healthcare, noting that their proposals have “good points” and “bad points.” In response to a request for comment on Sunday, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told NBC News, “As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” In Sunday’s “Meet the Press” interview, El-Sayed said he did see an opening to working with Trump, telling moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, the president signaled openness to the opportunity, and you know I played lacrosse growing up, and I was always taught that you play the ball, not the man. My job is to make sure that we’re advancing the goal to get everybody in this country healthcare.” The senator-elect also clarified that while he supports “Medicare for All,” the specific proposal he’d like to see advance is one offering a public option for insurance. “What I’d like to see is somewhat like thinking about health insurance like public schools,” El-Sayed said. “Everybody is entitled to public schools. Some people send their kids to private schools, but the next day, if they wanted to, they could send their kids to public schools. Everybody is entitled to it. That’s how I’m thinking about public health insurance under Medicare for All. Everybody’s entitled.” “I think it’s about the guarantee and the security that it offers,” he added.

articles.title: Yenesi, de ‘La bola negra’: “Las fachas van todas siempre a votar. Tenemos que ir porque si no nos comen”
articles.standfirst: La actriz pidió a sus fans que acudan a votar el 29N
articles.summary: La actriz pidió a sus fans que acudan a votar el 29N
articles.body: El próximo 29 de noviembre (29N), España se enfrenta a una de las elecciones generales más tensas de toda la historia de la democracia, con dos bandos muy diferenciados que, incluso, están haciendo que entre la sociedad se formen estos dos grupos de igual manera. La actriz de ‘La bola negra’, Yenesi, quien interpreta a Goyita, pidió a sus fans en su última entrevista que acudan a votar en los comicios: “Que vayan a votar, que vayan a votar, porque ahora nos toca”, señaló. Mostrando, claramente, su tendencia política, más cercana a la izquierda: “Todo el mundo votando, votando bien, que las fachas van todas siempre a votar. A las fachas no les importa, pero no lo piensan mucho. Nosotras tenemos que ir, porque si no nos comen, que ya veis cómo están las calles. No me jodáis. Id a votar”, sentenció. Y es que, son muchas las personalidades que han pedido el voto públicamente, como es el caso de la cantante Aitana. En su caso, se pronunció el pasado miércoles, 18 de noviembre, tras recibir el premio ‘Mujer del Año’ en los GQ Men of the Year 2026, celebrados en el Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía de Madrid. "Cada vez tengo más claro que me gustaría vivir en una sociedad que, aunque pensemos diferente, tengamos todos empatía, que se respeten los derechos de todo el mundo y, sobre todo, que sigamos avanzando y no retrocediendo, por favor", fueron sus palabras. “Me es inevitable pensar sobre todo en gente de mi generación a la que le es imposible independizarse, a la que le es imposible vivir una vida tranquila, aunque trabaje muchísimo y a la que le es imposible pensar en un futuro sin incertidumbre. Seguimos viviendo con miedo. Seguimos viviendo con violencia y seguimos viviendo en desigualdad”, sentenció.

articles.title: DHS, Dem officials clash after ICE arrest at Seattle airport
articles.summary: DHS says a passenger threw hot coffee at ICE officers during a Seattle airport arrest of a visa overstay, as Washington Democrats blast the operation.
articles.body: Federal officials and Washington state Democrats are at odds after ICE officers arrested two prospective airline travelers – both accused of overstaying visas and one accused of throwing hot coffee at agents – on a Seattle airport jetway Saturday morning. "This violence must end," the Department of Homeland Security fired back on X, responding to Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson saying, "ICE is completely and totally out of control." The operation began around 8:05 a.m. PT as travelers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight, according to the Department of Homeland Security. DHS says ICE officers targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, whom the agency described as a Mexican national "who overstayed his visa." During the arrest, other travelers began getting in the officers' way, and one passenger threw hot coffee at the agents, DHS said. TLAIB MOVES TO BLOCK ICE AIRPORT ARRESTS, SAYS TSA HELPING TARGET IMMIGRANTS "The individual who threw the hot coffee was identified as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, an illegal alien from Mexico and visa overstay," DHS wrote on X. "She was subsequently arrested as well. She will be charged with assaulting a federal officer." The post came in response to Ferguson, who claimed law enforcement removing suspected illegal immigrants from flights is "creating chaos in our communities." "ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson wrote on X, making no mention to the alleged assault of the officers. "Like many Americans, I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities." BORDER CZAR TOM HOMAN FIRES BACK AFTER DEMOCRAT CHRIS MURPHY CLAIMS ICE IS ‘TERRORIZING LITTLE KIDS’ Ferguson even suggested airlines should push federal immigration agents out of the airport, which has been under stress from this month's nationwide ground stop and rooting out security threats during the busy holiday travel season. "This morning, masked ICE agents terrorized our community, dragging at least one woman on the ground and arresting her as she was in line to board her flight," Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., wrote on X. "This behavior is totally unacceptable. Violent arrests are the hallmark of fascist states, not a democracy." At his Saturday news conference, Ferguson called video of the incident "horrific" and "chilling," adding that he told Alaska Airlines representatives that "they need to call on ICE to get out of our airports." He said he plans to make the same request of every other airline operating out of the Seattle and Tacoma airport. DHS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials have been agitated by protesters and efforts to halt the Trump administration's detention efforts, sometimes creating deadly circumstances and exchanges between federal officers and agitators. DEMS SHAMED AS DHS BRINGS ICE SHOOTING RECEIPTS AFTER POLITICIAN CALLED ICE OFFICERS ‘LIARS WITH MASKS’ DHS defended the agents and pointed to what it described as a surge in violence against federal officers, citing DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin's directive on prosecutions. "Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime and a felony," the DHS X post continued. "Secretary Mullin has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. Our brave law enforcement is facing more than a 1,600% increase in assaults, 300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats against them. This violence must end." Democrats ran on affordability in the midterm elections, but Jayapal vows to work to end immigration enforcement operations, taking the fight from American streets and airports to the House and Senate. 'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT SLAMMED BY TRUMP ADMIN FOR MOST 'RADICAL' PLAN TARGETING ICE YET "Soon, Democrats will take back control of Congress and we will continue the critical work to rein in these out of control agents and hold them accountable," her X post continued, expressing concern for the illegals who overstayed their visa versus the law enforcement officers attacked during an obstruction. "My heart goes out to those directly affected, and the passengers and airline workers whom ICE traumatized today." Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, a democratic socialist, called efforts to enforce immigration law "un-American." "I am outraged by videos of masked ICE agents causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway at Sea-Tac airport," she wrote Saturday on X. "These tactics are unacceptable and un-American." Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., called federal law enforcement "a profound threat to our community." "This morning, masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport," he wrote on X. "The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody. Let me be clear: this is absolutely unacceptable. "ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities. I am incredibly concerned about the conduct of immigration enforcement and believe that ICE is operating as a paramilitary force that is a profound threat to our community. There is no question that this agency needs to be reined in before causing more chaos and fear." DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE Alaska Airlines said it had no advance warning of the enforcement action and moved many affected passengers onto other flights. "Alaska Airlines was not provided advance notice of the enforcement action and we are working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred," the airline said in a statement, adding it is "concerned" by the federal action. Union leaders representing airport workers also criticized the timing of the arrests ahead of a busy travel week. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, called the operation a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos into the terminal. articles.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says ‘momentum is in our direction’ in battle for majority leader
articles.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said “momentum is in our direction” on his bid to serve as the Senate majority leader in the next Congress
articles.body: Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that “momentum is in our direction” in his bid for Senate majority leader. Asked directly how much support he had within the Democratic caucus, Van Hollen said the number is “north of 15” although it’s short of the 28 votes needed to win the leadership race against Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Democratic senators and senators-elect will hold a vote in December to determine the next majority leader, a dominant role in shaping the party’s agenda and its response to the Trump administration. Van Hollen’s allies have sought to frame him as a leader who can push for change, while Schumer’s allies have argued that his leadership helped usher in historic Democratic wins across the country. Asked whether he believes he can secure enough votes, Van Hollen said yes. “Yes, because if you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change,” he said in the Sunday interview. “They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate.” Van Hollen also said he believes the Democratic Party is “on probation” and needs to earn Americans’ trust. “You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual,” he said. Van Hollen said he personally believes that the filibuster, which requires that most bills in the Senate need at least 60 votes to pass, “is an anti-democratic provision.” “But I also understand that the job of the majority leader is to work with the caucus,” he continued. “So we should set sort of standards and criteria for at what level of obstruction by Republicans — to root out political corruption, to move forward on voting rights — at what level will we consider alternatives?” he said, listing two major policy fights for which Democrats could potentially change the rules. One possibility, he said, is requiring a talking filibuster so that Republicans would have to show their opposition to popular proposals on the Senate floor. Van Hollen, who has been floated as a potential presidential candidate, also confirmed on “Meet the Press” that he will not run for president, even if he loses the leadership race. Van Hollen initially said he was “kicking the tires” on a presidential run, but after jumping in the Senate leadership race, he said he was not pursuing a presidential run anymore. “After I saw the scope of this victory, this call from the American people, my view is now we have to deliver, we have to earn people’s trust, and that would be my focus entirely,” he said. “So no, I’m not running for president in 2028.”

articles.title: Progressives unveil $25 minimum wage push to solve affordability crisis despite economist inflation warning
articles.summary: House Democrats push a $25 minimum wage to fight the affordability crisis, but Heritage economist E.J. Antoni warns it could raise costs and unemployment.
articles.body: House Democrats are pushing to raise the federal minimum wage to $25 an hour, calling the current hourly pay a "remnant of slavery" to "oppress women," despite warnings from conservative economists that the proposal could drive up costs and threaten jobs. The proposal from the Congressional Progressive Caucus would more than triple the current $7.25 federal minimum wage, raising questions about its potential impact on businesses and workers in states with significantly lower living costs than major cities. "We should be rallying around (a minimum wage of) $25 at minimum, and it should be cost adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., told Fox News Digital. AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST? Asked whether a nationwide $25 minimum wage could hurt workers and businesses in lower-cost states, Blair argued that the proposed rate should serve as a national baseline. The congressman said $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living." Blair acknowledged concerns that raising the minimum wage could contribute to inflation but said lawmakers must find a way to increase workers' earnings while "keeping people afloat." Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., echoed Blair's support for the proposal, pointing to the high cost of living in cities such as Seattle and Washington, D.C., as justification for raising wages. DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD "The truth is that the boogeyman, the corporations, don't want to pay their workers liveable wages," Ramirez told Fox News Digital. Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J. Antoni warned that a $25 federal minimum wage could increase costs and unemployment, arguing that the economic consequences would extend beyond major metropolitan areas. "Whenever a price floor on labor is set above the market equilibrium, a surplus of labor is created. In this case, we call that surplus unemployment," Antoni told Fox News Digital. DEMOCRATS PLOT MASSIVE SPENDING SPREE AFTER MIDTERM ROUT — AND TRUMP COULD HELP THEM PULL IT OFF Despite those warnings, progressive lawmakers expressed confidence that the proposal could gain support from Democratic leadership in both chambers and potentially reach President Donald Trump's desk. "There's a widespread coalition of folks in the Democratic caucus who have long been saying that one job should be enough to pay the bill," Blair told Fox News Digital. Ramirez also expressed cautious optimism about the possibility of Trump signing the legislation, pointing to his previous willingness to discuss bipartisan immigration reform. She said she "never knows what the president might or might not be willing to do." SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS The Living Wage for All coalition, which joined lawmakers in unveiling the proposal, says support for a $25 minimum wage extends beyond Democratic voters. "Not a blue wave," the coalition said, citing polling it claimed showed 63% of Republicans support a $25 federal minimum wage. "There is a blue collar demand that says that this is how we address the affordability crisis." Coalition members also drew comparisons between the history of minimum-wage policies and slavery-era labor practices, arguing that the current wage system has historically disadvantaged women and marginalized workers. The proposal comes as Democrats prepare to advance their affordability agenda in the 120th Congress, with progressives seeking to make higher wages a central component of the party's economic platform. articles.title: Trump says it would be 'hard' to work with Chuck Schumer: 'He will fail again'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says it will be "hard" to work with Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader, claiming the Democratic leader will "fail again."
articles.body: President Donald Trump predicted it would be "hard" to work with Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., if he is chosen to continue leading Senate Democrats next year. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday that Schumer is likely to "fail again" if he is elected. Schumer is running for Senate majority leader once again, but opposition to his leadership is gaining steam. "It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader. He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again," Trump wrote. DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES "All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one. articles.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 19...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."

Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins , which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast , as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change."

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration , going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."

After House Speaker Mike Johnson , R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's high-water marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

articles.title: Chuck Hubbard defeats Rep. Virginia Foxx after a recount in their North Carolina House race
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, defeating veteran Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerf...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Chuck Hubbard was elected to the House from North Carolina, defeating veteran Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, who chairs the powerful House Rules Committee.

Foxx said in a statement Sunday that she called Hubbard to concede after a recount failed to close the narrow gap between them. Hubbard leads by 330 votes out of 287,000 cast.

Foxx was first elected to the House in 2004. The 5th Congressional District covers a rural stretch of western North Carolina.

"The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government, and I am proud to be a citizen of a nation that prizes fair and free elections," Foxx said in a statement.

Hubbard is a longtime journalist who got his start working for the local newspaper owned by members of his family.

"Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices," he wrote in a post on X.

Hubbard's victory is the capstone to a larger Democratic rout in North Carolina — and deep wins nationally — in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, giving the party control of the House and Senate when the next Congress convenes in January.

Roy Cooper, the state's former governor, won election to the Senate, becoming the first Democrat elected to the chamber since 2008. And Democratic candidates won 11 of the state's 14 House seats despite redistricting efforts that were meant to give Republicans an advantage.

articles.title: Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian in New York state Senate history
articles.summary: Kawas, a democratic socialist, won with 74.5 percent of the vote, championing progressive politics.
articles.body:
New York City, United States – “You have all elected the first Palestinian in New York Senate history!” Aber Kawas shouted over cheers to hundreds of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members at a bar on election night.

As chants of “Aber! Aber! Aber!” filled the patio of Bohemia Beer Garden on November 3, media cameras flashed against her shiny blazer, embroidered with traditional Palestinian tatreez in gold and red.

Kawas, 34, made history as the first Palestinian , and the first Muslim woman, in the New York state Senate and the state legislature. She won the seat representing district 12 in northwest Queens, home to one of New York City’s largest Arab communities, where nearly half of residents were born outside the United States.

As her speech ended and chants of “Free, Free Palestine” rang through the garden, Stylianos Karolidis, a DSA organiser on Kawas’s team, stepped up to remind supporters that she really, really had not wanted to run for office. The DSA had to “hound her non-stop” until she acquiesced, he said.

Kawas had worked with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when he was in the state legislature, so they knew her organising skills.

Kawas said she did not initially think it was possible to run for office without compromising her commitment to Palestinian liberation. Her victory, with 74.5 percent of the vote against Republican Han Khon To, was part of a broader tide of wins for pro-Palestine and democratic socialist candidates in the midterm elections, including Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Mayor-elect Nithya Raman in Los Angeles, California.

“This midterm election showed a politics of human rights that includes Palestinians is a winning platform,” said Institute for Middle East Understanding policy project executive director Margaret DeReus. “For millions of Americans, holding Israel accountable for genocide and supporting Palestinian freedom are the litmus test.”

Days after the election, Kawas reflected on the DSA’s first approach and her doubts about entering a political system she had long distrusted. In her Queens home, a poster honouring Palestinians who had been killed hung above shelves of books on Islamic liberation, the Palestinian movement and US politics. But she ran because the political climate had shifted, she told Al Jazeera.

“It felt like being pro-Palestinian was the most important thing to run on.”

Kawas’s parents were uprooted from their homes in Palestine during the mass expulsions. Her father was uprooted in 1948 and her mother in 1967. They grew up as neighbours in Jordan before falling in love, marrying and moving to the US with their infant son in the 1990s. They later had three daughters. Aber is the third child of the four, sandwiched between her two sisters. “Which is why I have a lot of politician skills,” she said, laughing.

But when she was in the seventh grade, her father was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which her mother described as a regular occurrence in New York’s post-9/11 Muslim community. His detention meant weekend visits to prison, and it left the family struggling.

“I had to work whether I wanted to or not; you have to become both man and woman, father and mother,” her mother, Manal Abu Samaha, told Al Jazeera.

When Kawas was a teenager, she said she travelled to Albany to tell her family’s story, hoping to expand opportunities for undocumented students like her older brother, who was ineligible for a college scholarship. Lawmakers seemed uninterested, Kawas recalls.

The state senator-elect credits the experience with launching her advocacy career and shaping her goals as a politician. “It’s not upending systems, but it’s meeting real, immediate material needs for people,” she said. “That’s maybe a little kernel of what got me to run.”

Backed by Mamdani and the DSA, Kawas’s campaign said it mobilised more than 1,000 volunteers to knock on doors, make calls and campaign on affordable housing, healthcare and public transport, as well as the Palestinian solidarity work that has shaped her life.

Kawas recalled that, while Mamdani was warned that supporting Palestine would end his political career, the stance instead helped him earn voters’ trust. Seeing this, she said, made her less wary that entering politics would require her to compromise her beliefs.

“I voted for Aber Kawas because Palestinian liberation is not separate from the everyday survival and basic needs that Americans and New Yorkers struggle with,” said community organiser Doreen Mohammed. “Aber Kawas’s vocal support for Palestine is what we need more of everywhere.”

Kawas told Al Jazeera she believes her stance on Palestine helped her earn trust from local leaders. Whether it can change US policy is a harder question.

“Many of us are rightfully cautious, if not outright sceptical, when it comes to electoral politics,” said Samee Sulaiman, an anthropologist at Columbia University who studies the Middle East. “Can we build and use this nascent power to finally end American support of Israel in every way? This will be the real test.”

Kawas acknowledged that a lot will depend on the political will of legislative leaders.

“The challenge, truly, is going to be the political will of the leadership,” she said. “We [the DSA] are still a minority in the legislature.”

Her first priority is reviving the Not on Our Dime! bill, which she drafted with then-Assembly member Zohran Mamdani in 2023 to prohibit New York non-profits from supporting illegal Israeli settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territory. Rejected at the time, it is now back before the New York state Senate.

Kawas said she remains convinced change is possible, pointing to the activists who helped bring an end to apartheid in South Africa.

“If there’s the power of the people behind you, that is what you carry with you, and that’s who you’ll be accountable to.”

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992
articles.summary: Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep.
articles.body: Democrat Chuck Hubbard has defeated GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx for a congressional seat in North Carolina, NBC News projects, adding to a Democratic wave that is projected to deliver the party at least 258 House seats. It’s the largest House majority that any party has held this century, according to the Office of the House Historian, and four races are yet to be called. It’s also the largest Democratic majority since 1992, when the party also won 258 seats. The second-largest House majority for Democrats this century came in 2008, when the party won 257 seats. The party cemented control of the chamber not only by winning competitive races in battleground districts, but also by winning in deeply Republican areas that voted for President Donald Trump by double-digit margins just two years ago. In 2024, Trump won Foxx’s district by almost 18 percentage points, per an NBC News Decision Desk analysis. Now, Hubbard is projected to win North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District by a fraction of a percentage point following a recount that Foxx requested after Election Day. Earlier Sunday, Foxx called Hubbard to concede, according to a source familiar with the call. In a post on X, Hubbard wrote: “Earlier today I spoke with Congresswoman Virginia Foxx who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process. Let me be the first to thank Congresswoman Foxx for her decades of service and countless sacrifices.” Foxx isn’t the only North Carolina Republican who lost in what was considered to be a solidly GOP seat heading into Election Day. Democrats flipped seven Republican seats in North Carolina, the most of any state in the nation. In the state’s 9th Congressional District, Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda II defeated GOP Rep. Richard Hudson, who this year chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. Elsewhere in the state, Democratic Rep.-elect Cyril Jefferson defeated GOP Rep. Addison McDowell. Trump won Hudson’s district by 16 percentage points in 2024 and McDowell’s district by 17 percentage points that year.

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.
